source.title: What Can Transformer Learn with Varying Depth? Case Studies on Sequence Learning Tasks

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines depth on synthetic sequence-learning tasks, not power-law scaling of held-out language-model pretraining loss, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. It mentions Kaplan et al. in connection with scalability but does not test or rely on the scaling-law findings.
record.gate_note: The experiments vary attention-layer counts and report performance on synthetic tasks. These results concern task learnability by depth, rather than the claim's scaling laws. The paper cites Kaplan et al.; cited results are not extracted as study findings.
record.test_reason: The paper proves and checks which synthetic sequence tasks attention-only transformers can solve at 1, 2 and 3 layers. It reports no held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute, no extrapolation, no compute-optimal allocation and no shape-at-fixed-parameter comparison. Kaplan et al. is cited only in the discussion, as something the depth thresholds might help explain. The loss curves in Figure 2 are training-loss trajectories over steps for one task, not scaling fits.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors add that one layer cannot perfectly solve the reasoning and generalization tasks: the reasoning accuracy of any single-layer transformer is bounded at 3/4 on a toy construction. They also say extra heads help memorization but barely affect reasoning and generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies theoretical constructions and experiments on synthetic sequence tasks, not the original scaling-law measurement procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Task type and attention-layer count affect the reported task performance. The paper also reports that additional heads have little significant impact on its reasoning and generalization tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic tasks, the success of attention-only transformers depends on depth. One layer memorizes but performs at random-guess level on reasoning and template generalization. Two layers solve those tasks. Contextual generalization needed three layers, and four layers learned it faster (Appendix B.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The minimum transformer depth needed for a task depends on the task's compositional complexity; extra heads matter little for reasoning and generalization tasks.

record.problems: The experiments use synthetic tasks rather than language-model pretraining and do not measure held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation. Depth comparisons do not hold parameter count fixed. The text reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant scaling-law results were reported. The paper's plotted training-loss trajectories are not extracted as scaling-law evidence; the text does not give numerical loss values for them.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining-loss power law in N, D or C.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: depth changes task success on synthetic tasks, but parameter count is not held fixed and there is no language-model loss.
All: no power-law fits in any regime.
All: no downstream-versus-scale or downstream-versus-loss trend; the depth thresholds are discrete capability results.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/cites_only classification is right. The models are attention-only: the MLP layers are removed, ReLU attention is used, and the first layer is initialised with the constructed weight pattern (Appendix B.1), which limits how far the results generalise. No row bears on any claim version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss power laws in parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture effects on loss at fixed parameter count; the study varies depth on synthetic tasks and does not hold parameter count fixed.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.
